Ok... this is NOT exactly the skip it of my youth... but after purchasing many disappointing knock-offs that broke immediately or didn't work because of basic design falls....and "modern" versions that also don't work (twister skip it- the dingle is WAY too heavy and the "cord" is twisted and doesn't want to fly around your ankle), avoiding still others due to horrible reviews and looking on ebay and finding one that was CLOSE for $120!!! .... I found this one... No reviews... I admit, I was scared... plus I worried about the knobby bouncy ball... but EUREKA!! It works!! Listen it lights up and eventually it will die as the batteries are not replaceable... but WHO CARES? You can STILL skip it! I am LOVING this. Wish I was still as young and bouncy as I used to be 40 years ago... but I adored it then and now. I just can't do it for hours like I used to...and I'm a bit slower. :) I'm pretty sure this counts as exercise and it's fun! Of course, mine is covered in sand cause I skip on the wide open beach. If you were a fan of the original, you'll find this amusing and it works! I'm getting two more... one for my sister (else she WILL steal mine) and one for the house that isn't covered with sand. :) You do need a pretty good size area that is clear... but it works on floors or carpets and sand of course. I'm pretty sure people think it's very amusing to see an old, fat lady skipping down the beach. HA!
The loop is plenty big enough to slip over your shoe... 5 1/2" diameter on the side of the plastic ankle loop... the cord is tube covered (this is REALLY important because otherwise the cord just wraps around your ankle and you can't "skip it").... the ball is attached to cord very well... I yanked on it... stood and pulled... obviously more than you need to do... but I wanted to test it.
You don't get to pick your color... doesn't bother me. I got a really great purple one in my first order.
I will update if there are any breakage issues, but honestly it's pretty dang well made and I don't expect those kinds of issues.

I never really played Uno much as a child, but when I saw that a popular kids card game had been adapted for younger children, I was excited to try it. We've tried a few simple kids card games with our four-year-old daughter, but the combination of basic strategy, attempting to hold a hand of cards, and keeping cards private has proved to be a bit too much at this stage. The designers of this adaptation were clearly aware of these challenges, and this game addresses them all.

Keeping cards/pieces private has been sacrificed in the attempt to make this game kid friendly, but I don't think that's a problem. In fact, it was the only way we were able to play most card games anyways. Mattel used to make a version of this game that had little fences for hiding each player's pieces; you could always borrow that approach and use your own make-shift barricades if you're playing with older kids.

This adaptation also does away with the challenge of holding a hand of cards. Instead, kids have large plastic pieces that are easy to grab and can be laid out in front of the player instead of being constantly held like cards. These plastic pieces also have the benefit of standing up to use better than cards, which three and four year olds have a tendency to bend.

And, the gameplay is simple enough for a three year old to understand with just enough strategy to hold the interest of kids a few years older as well. The youngest kids can should be able to follow the basic rules easily, while those a bit older can put a bit more thought into how they play their hand.

The carrying case that is integrated into the game play is also a great feature. There is zero setup required; just open the box and start playing.

While a more cynical consumer might see this game as a way for Mattel to squeeze a few more dollars out of each sale, I think this adaptation of the Uno card game for younger players is a great addition to our daughter's game collection (other favorites include [[ASIN:B002V3RCE6 Busytown]], [[ASIN:B00005NQE8 Hiss]], and [[ASIN:B00HN2BXUY Robot Turtles]]).

B00RHGG3JC.text: This is a  fine art set for kids, though I do have a couple of concerns.  First, the positive:  The set is well packaged.  The pencils are vibrant on the page, unlike some less expensive colored pencils.  The pastels are nice, with an even greater variety of colors.  The set includes drawing paper and sandpaper.  However, there are just a couple of minor negatives:  The set is targeted at really young children, and I do not think most of them would have the small motor skills to manipulate such slim pencils and narrow pastels.  The right age is probably about eight.  I also think the set is somewhat overpriced.  You could get each of these items separately (and much more drawing paper) for less money.  That said, this is a nice set for a budding artist.  It would make a good gift, especially if you like all the materials in well packaged in one place.

The quality of these products are good for the price, but the selection is odd for a starter set. Pastels are difficult for a young child to use. The color pencils are odd colors, not the primary colors you would expect in a starter set. The blending stump and sandpaper are also complicated for a younger child. The description says ages 3 and up, but I think this set is way to complicated for age 3-7. Maybe this is OK for age 8-11 as an addition to a more basic set that they are outgrowing. Ages 12 and up are probably going to want a set with more variety. Also note that 30% of your 40 piece set is 12 sheets of drawing paper. I would have given this set 1 more star if it had a better description of who should use it.

Based on the reviews, I was a little disappointed in the quality of the colored pencils. They're basic! Still, this is a nice set for a younger child. My 5 year old is beyond thrilled with it.

This set comes with CHALK pastels. For some reason, I was expecting oil pastels. Since we didn't already have any chalk pastels in our home, and have a beautiful chalk pastel book waiting to give us advice, these will be put to good use.

I'd recommend adding a lovely drawing pad to go along with this set. It does come with one, but it's small and only 12 pages. A young artist will use those pages up in no time.

This set also comes with a sanding block, a kneaded eraser, a metal pencil sharpener, and a blending stick.

For a younger child, this is a nice set, but if that child has already been drawing and is more practiced with art, this might not be the best choice.

This is a very nice set of pencils and pastels.  I was just at Michaels and they wanted $12 dollars for 8 pencils so this is a much better buy.  The set comes with a sharpener and a wide range of colors to choose from.  My tween is into coloring and drawing so she was really excited to get this product.

The main issue I have with this is that is is not meant for young users (even though it is advertised for them). No toddler is going to be able to use the blending stump or really understand how to use the pastels. Instead, this is a much nicer product for the older user -someone who would enjoy blending colors and using the eraser and so on.

The other weird thing is that the the box advertises itself as a "40 piece" drawing set; That is really misleading as 12 of the 40 pieces are sheets of paper. (Really? C'mon guys!)

The paper pad is useful only in that it is like having (low-end) batteries included when you get a toy. You appreciate that they are there, and you can get started right away, but you know you'll need to upgrade to better batteries as soon as they run out. In other words, I recommend buying a larger paper pad (size-wise, and paper sheet quantity-wise) along with this product so that you can really get the best use out of everything.

As for their quality? I was not disappointed. The items all seem well made and are packaged nicely (which is why I thought they'd make a nice gift).

Overall, and for the older children (instead of the youngest ones) I recommend this.

ALEX offers several different artist drawing sets, some with more items included than others  This is a medium-sized set which has 40 pieces. It includes pencils and pastels. Some of the others have much more variety, so it all depends on what you want.

For the price, this is a good set. If your budding artist is interested in learning to use pastels (these are chalk, not oil), this would be a good set for starting. I was disappointed that the drawing pad included is so small and wonder why a larger one could not have been included as well. Frankly, the small pad is too small for the pastels. Make sure to buy a pad of larger paper; better still if you can get pastel paper.

The pencils come in basic colors and can be blended to make more colors. I would definitely encourage your child to learn how to blend and blur using the blending stump. If these resources inspire your artist, I would encourage you to invest in good quality pastels and pencils. But this kit is a great starting place!

This is a great set for younger kids - it's not quite artist quality, but it's much more advanced than most of the stuff out there, with colored pencils, chalk pastels, a blending stump, kneaded eraser, and a sandpaper block. Great for the price. Given as a gift to our tween-aged nephew who is just learning about art. But it's wonderful value at such a low cost, especially as an introductory tool for younger artists.

Came in time for Christmas.  The kids really loved it. All together ordered 3 art sets for the kids for Christmas, including a more expensive one that came in a wood case. But they liked this one the best because of the clay/squishy stuff that comes in it.

Overall I'm a fan of the original Apples To Apples, but I've found it can get very repetitive fairly quickly as the same types of cards are used over time. This new edition aims to remove that problem by letting players write in their own answers.

There's two ways to play here: either one judge pulls a freestyle card with a blank spot in a sentence and reads it aloud, then everyone else writes whatever word they think is funniest on the dry erase apple boards, or instead one judge writes any word on an apple card and the rest of the players choose a freestyle card that humorously matches. The first mode is more fun for people who like to come up with silly things on the fly, while the second is better for those who don't want to be put on the spot.

With the blank spots and ability to write in answers, it appears this is sort of a sly attempt for Apples To Apples to take on the Cards Against Humanity crowd, because the game goes out of its way to make it easy to be dirty. Without question, the vast majority of the blank spots on the cards are aimed at easily being filled with any given euphemism for “penis.” Here's a sampling of random freestyle cards I just pulled from the deck:

“I wouldn't want to be caught holding BLANK,” “It feels good to rub your face against a smooth BLANK,” “Nothing feels better than BLANK,” “The most important ingredient in a romantic evening is BLANK,” “I would never want a monkey to get its paws on my BLANK,” and so on. For the twisted Cards Against Humanity players, there's then also cards like “A family reunion is a great place to find BLANK.”

That being said, this is solid fun for younger kids or adults who aren't interested in that kind of game, as you can tailor it to any given group just by changing what you write. Our group did some non-horrifyingly offensive rounds just for fun and it worked just as well. It's a laugh riot having people try to come up with cards that match the random phrases you come up with - “time traveling nazi assassin” or “homeless badgers” for instance.

There's only two downsides to the game – first up, the packaging is terrible. The box is clearly not meant to continue holding the cards and markers after being opened. Get yourself some ziploc bags or a plastic carrying case with dividers to store the game's parts. Second, for no apparent reason two of the apple cards meant to be written on have sample text printed on them, which was a terrible idea, as it essentially means you've got two less cards for extra players. You could technically use them in a game, but you'll have to shuffle the apple cards each round and re-hand them out, otherwise it will be obvious who is handing in the cards with the pre-printed text at the top every single round.

The original Apples to Apples is a game that's provided me with hours of fun, both when playing with family members and when playing with friends. The game is a favorite with almost everyone I know, so I was eager to try out this new spin on the game.

A big downside to this game is the packaging. This may not sound like a big deal, but the old boxes for both the original game and the kids' version kept all the cards nice and neat. Once you've taken out the bubble packaging for this game, you're left with a pretty flimsy plastic box in which the cards, mini-markers, and write-on boards get all jumbled together. Plus, the box is much larger than its contents, so it takes up a lot of space. This is a downside for me, because it means I need to find some other means of storing the game.

Gameplay is fun. This version comes with a big stack of cards with lots of prompts for creating your own answers. The one hurdle to this is that if you're playing with people who know your handwriting, it's obvious which answer is yours, unlike with the previous versions where there's no way of telling who threw which card into the mix once they're all shuffled. We also quickly decided against shuffling the boards as we were afraid it would rub the answers off and make them hard to read. It probably goes without saying that when you play this game you need some damp paper towel and/or a damp rag to clean off the boards, so it's messier than the original game.

Taking the anonymity away is a downside as part of the fun of the game is finding out after the fact who chose which answer, and it also prevents whoever is judge from demonstrating a bias toward any particular players. It is sometimes hard to come up with responses on the fly, and if you're not a particularly creative person, this might not be much fun for you. With the original game, you have a set number of answers to choose from, so you just have to go with whatever is in your hand.

All in all, this is a decent game, but I prefer the original.

The VTech Spinning Lights Learning Hippo is a cute and fun toy for any child from 18 months to 4 years. It’s a portable vocabulary building that can engage kids with six different activities to help language development and introduce numbers. The design is simple and fun and as kids pull the bird down from the hippo’s back and it will repeat letters, use phonics to help kids learn, and much more. The hippo even asks questions to help reinforce the learning experience. Kids love the ABC button, which they can sing along with. This hippo is a great reinvention of a classic spin toy with a ton more abilities designed to help your kid grow and develop to the best of their ability.

B01ATI9364.text: My great-grandson liked this a lot and really enjoyed riding it.  He's not a large kid, but is one year older than the recommended ages for the toy.  He is within the weight limit, which I think is 50 pounds or under.  He can probably enjoy it for about a year, but he was almost too big for it now so you probably don't want to get this for a child who is approaching the upper age limit, which I think the box said was 5.  Also, if you have a big child close to the maximum age and maximum weight, they might not fit the toy.  At around a $200 price, I consider this to be a luxury toy and you might be able to find toys for a lot less that would be just as much fun for a kid.  I recommend getting it for kids at the lower end of the age range (2 or 3), so they can enjoy it for a few years before they outgrow it.  Of course you can always donate it when they do outgrow it.  Not much to assemble on it and the few parts that need to be put on are easy to install.  The only real downside to this toy is the initial charge time of 18 hours.  Kids are impatient (some adults are too) and if you present this to them and then they find out they can't use it until the next day, there could be some disappointment.  Of course that could be a way to teach patience too.  After the initial overnight charge, the battery seemed to last quite well, so they should be able to enjoy a driving session until they lose interest and a recharge is needed.  This is not huge, but it is a large item that you need a storage place for and a place to plug it in while it is charging.  As several reviewers have said, this works better on hard surfaces.  This doesn't move very fast, but fast enough for younger kids; older kids might find it too slow.  Obviously too, as a kid gets older they might not find a toy like this that "cool".  Since this is a motorized riding toy, obviously you do need to supervise a kid while riding it, especially younger ones; don't buy it if you think you are going to turn your kid loose with it and not have to watch them.  You need adequate space in your house or a big driveway to use this, as you probably don't want the kids driving it in the street, unless you live in a very low traffic residential area and/or are right beside them when they are using it.  Probably best for use on sidewalks or a fenced yard if you are going to use it outside.  Keep in mind too that if you go any great distance away from your house and the charge runs out, you now have a 50 pound toy to somehow get home.  How noisy a toy is also can be a factor on whether you want to get it or not; this runs reasonably quiet, which is a plus.  A fun toy for the appropriately aged small child.

Let's Blllaaaaazzzzzeeee! This is the Power Wheels Blaz Monster Truck designed to help take kids all around Axle City! If you are not familiar with the show, Blaze is a happy go lucky Monster Truck always on the lookout to do tricks and help things in need. The show has a very heavy STEM influence and does a great job combining Monster Truck shenanigans with actual math and science concepts.

As far as this Blaze Power Wheels goes.... it is definitely smaller than I expected (and hoped). Our 6 year old daughter is definitely too large for it... she will fit (well she can squeeze into it), but Blaze probably tops out at 1mph with her in it.

Notes

- Assembly is not difficult, but it does take about 30 minutes. As someone else mentioned the decals are probably the hardest part. I gave up trying to get them on without air bubbles!

- The battery is tinsy. I haven't times battery life, but the battery is about 1/4 the size of what comes standard on the larger Power Wheels.

- The steering wheel has two buttons - one lets Blaze *rev up* and the other plays some of Blaze's fun phrases.

- Has both forward and reverse

- Has a small area in the back... not exactly a trunk... but it is a small flat spot where your child will happy store random things.... rocks, shovels, empty juice boxes, and etc.

- Speed - pretty slow... you should be able to easily walk alongside it.

Final Verdict - lots of fun for fans of Blaze BUT if your child is 4 or older you will likely ONLY get 1 year out of it before they outgrow it.

As a kid growing up I always wanted a motorized truck I could drive around in, up and down the block and around my back yard. Unfortunately Power Wheels did not exist when I was a kid. It came in a very large box, and was very easy to put together, a friend and I did it in about 10 minutes. The stickers are cute and really add to the look of Blaze!

The wheels are hard plastic, with no rubberized parts. This isn't an issue most of the time, but it makes it a bit harder to go up a steeper incline on pavement. It seems to run well on grass/dirt. The ride form my kids doesn't seem all that smooth, but the kids also don't seems to care, lol. My kids will run this until the battery dies and then want to ride more!

I purchased this for my grandson as this was the only present he wanted for his 4th birthday. It exceeded my expectations as far as battery charge sustainability (off and on use for two days before it needs charging). I am most impressed with its ability to go up inclines (on and off pavement) and through the back yard. It is also a nice touch that the hood raises to reveal an "engine", though it is all gray in color. You must lift the hood, unscrew two screws, and then plug in charger in order to charge. I don't care for that but being that it doesn't have to be charged every day it's okay. Then only truly negative feedback I have is with the decals. You must put those on yourself and we were unable to get them all on without bubbling. My grandson doesn't mind, but since the Blaze lacks other basic features (working lights or movable doors), it would be nice if the decals were perfect.

This monster is heavy (50 lb before you add another 20 lb of infant!), the tires are terrible, battery life is mysterious, and the product description implies that 50% of the population won't be able to use or enjoy it:

“Hold onto your hubcaps!” the Blaze monster truck from power wheels gives young boys the chance to pretend to be AJ and drive their very own Blaze! boys can have adventures driving around axle city on their very own Blaze monster truck 6VT!"
I guess girls are out of luck, huh?

When I tried to dig into the battery life issue, I couldn't figure out whether this is a lithium ion battery or a Nickel-based battery. The former are lightweight, but can be a fire hazard if cheaply designed. The latter are heavy and prone to the memory effect. Given the weight of this brute, I would guess these are Nickel-based rechargeable batteries. I did figure out that the battery only has a 6 month warranty, while the rest of the vehicle is covered for a year... To maximize battery life, always completely discharge before recharging to full.

B01BQ9S96A.text: This is an unexpectedly accurate Rogue One stormtrooper helmet for the price.  The fit for an adult is a bit tight, but can be worn without a problem if you adjust the straps to extend around the full circumference of the inside of the helmet.  With a proper fit your forehead and bridge of your nose will press against the front of the helmet.  Not particularly comfortable for wearing a long time, but allows moving your head without the helmet slipping.  The recessed "gills" of the tube stripes and the tears below the corners of the eyes are detail features unique to the R1 stormtrooper done well in this design.  The voice changer does work, though it's not that loud.  This is a sturdy heavy helmet at 2.2 pounds.  The 3-piece design easily snaps together, though does leave some visible seams, but not too bad.  But for the original price at release, this is a very good deal.
Product is nice for display but that is it! Voice changer didn't work out of the box. Definitely made for small kid not adult kid :(

Simply gorgeous looking. The best looking Stormtrooper helmet you will find at an affordable price. While likely not meeting the 501sts standards without some work, for anybody else it will be a magnificent piece to display or wear to torture the cat.

The helmet is three pieces, at least out of the box. Unlike some other adult helmet replicas, in which the separate pieces are used to get a better fit and close around the head, (Hasbro Legends Iron Man and Starlird, Bandai's Red Power Ranger) for the Stormtrooper helmet, the three pieces are largely for manufacture and shipping. Once you clap them together you will not be taking them apart. It goes on over the head,just as seen in the movies.

Fit and finish is superb. I can't speak to the minute accuracy of the sculpt, but to the inexpert eye it looks dead on. It's mainly unpainted white ABS plastic. Which is a good thing in this case. Stormtrooper gear is shiny white plastic. With some nice clean paint apps for detailing, such as the blue on the respirator vents and the grey temple and nose details. The lenses are dark green. I'm not sure if that is accurate to the on screen props, but they look right in the fles. Giving the shiny black look for the eyes with just enough color to make them seem real.

The voice changer is pure garbage. It sounds awful, randomly works and just seems tacked on. The only reason I don't take a star off for it is it is completely and utterly pointless and unnecessary. Nobody is buying this thing just to hear themselves say "these aren't the droids w're looking for" and "move along" through a cheesy toy voice box. Just leave the batteries out.

The fit on an adult male head is decent. The internal strapping is meh at best. It suffers for only being anchored to the front half of the helmet (due to the three piece design). Without a hear anchor on the head strap the helmet tends to tilt upwards slightly, limiting your downward vision. If you plan of routinely wearing this thing it would be worthwhile to invest in some cheap motorcycle of football helmet padding to put inside.

While it has a few minor flaws, the shear value of this thing cannot be beat. It's the helmet you have craved since that glorious May Day in 1978. A look and design that has honestly never been equaled. And it is available at a below $100 retail price. You can't beat that.

B01C64O9T0.text:
This is such an adorable toy. It is well made and loved.

The reason for 3 stars is the price. If this set was mostly wood, it would be worth the high price. It is a good quality plastic but still plastic. It should be priced according to the materials not the name. In my opinion, BRIO used to rise above other toys because it was made of wood, which could be passed down to the next child.

If you are not expecting a Brio wooden toy set, you may like this fire station set. Unfortunately, I was expecting wood, and I am disappointed. I assumed, wrongly, that this would be an old-fashioned, high-quality, Brio, wooden toy set. It is not! This fire station is almost entirely plastic, except for one small area. Yes, it is apparently a high-quality plastic, but it is still plastic. Wooden toys are sturdy and made to last across multiple generations. Plastic is not.

I personally think that, since this toy set is made of plastic, it is quite overpriced and not a good value. It is priced as if it were made of wood. Further, I wonder why on earth a company that is famed for its high-quality, wooden toys would opt to convert to plastic toys? It makes no sense.

However, if you are not looking for wooden toys for your child or grandchild, the fact that this is just another plastic toy set, in a world already over-filled with plastic, the plastic construction may not bother you. This toy set, on the positive side, does have very attractive, bright colors, and it does inspire creative play, as the older, wooden sets did. It's just not wood!

This set is for children age 3 and up because of small parts and a choking hazard.

This is a nice, cute fire station.  It has twelve pieces total.  It’s kind of small.  Most of it is plastic, though there are a couple of wooden pieces. BRIO sets are “expandable”, so you can add different sets together.  There are lots and lots of different add-on’s, so you can really go crazy with it.  Unfortunately, the sets are crazy expensive.  They are very good quality toys, but I can’t say that this set, for example, is worth over eighty bucks.

This little Central Fire Station is adorable! There's 12 pieces in the set. The main fire station, a slide, 2 vehicles, 2 firefighters, a fire flame, a tool box, a chain saw, and 2 flat pieces that slide attach to and attachment area. This is just one set. There's a HUGE collection of sets for the BRIO railroad. You can add different sets as desired for a huge display should you wish for a larger layout. We've purchased two wooden R/R sets as gits and the quality was top-notched. The Fire Station has great quality too. You won't be disappointed. So much FUN that us adults want to play too!

I LOVE Brio train sets, my little brother had a bunch and they were absolutely remarkable. They were wonderfully made, and the attention to detail was always amazing. I was very excited to see this, and then I was a little disappointed to see how light the box was when it came. The lighted car does work, and it's really neat, but the fire station itself is really lightweight plastic with absolutely no heft to it. Of course the kids don't care at all, and that's fine. But for what this costs, it's a little bit of a let-down.

Bought this as a birthday present for our grandson....the seller shipped it without putting it in a shipping box, without even wrapping it.  The shipping label was slapped right onto the box itself.  The box was not even taped shut and there's a big hole in the box.  We took a quick look in the box and it appears the items are OK; but, since it's a gift, we didn't want to pull everything out since the pieces are packed with the manufacturer's wrapping, etc.  Hoping everything is there and it's frustrating that there's a big hole in a box with a shipping label when we're giving it as a present.  Brio items are awesome, the 1-star rating is for the seller.

This fire station set is so cute and interactive. Perfect for all kids, any occasion. The thing I love about this the most is the tracks are universal and connect with many of the other wooden train track sets out there making it a great way to add to the collection. The price feels steep for what you get, so I'm taking a star off for that. Right now, the price is sitting around $80-90 and it just feels a bit steep to me.
The set comes with what is pictured on the box, making a nice set for pretend play. The set also connects to others in the series, letting your little one make a town of sorts.

Brio makes toys of exceptional quality. They're extremely well made and designed to withstand the abuse of childhood.

This little fire station is just wonderful. It comes with the pieces needed to put together the station as shown on the box, two vehicles, two firefighters, a "fire", a case and a chainsaw. The vehicles are impressively detailed; one featuring lights and sound and a hose on a little functioning reel. My son has had fun playing with this station, although the excitement of it alone is somewhat brief for the price. This one is really designed to be added to other track sets to create a larger world of play. Included in this set is exactly one piece of track, which is just enough to connect this station into an existing track system. If you want this to be a standalone toy, you'll either want to not attach the piece of track or prepare to spend more on additional track.

My only complaint is the price. If you really want to get into this line of train tracks and accessories, you can expect to easily spend into the several hundreds. There are less expensive options out there with matched quality to this set. For the price of this toy alone, it would've been nice of them to include enough track to make a small loop at least.

All in all we love the fire station but the price prevents me from giving a full five stars. If the companion sets were reasonably priced I'd consider them but at the price point of this line I doubt we'll be purchasing additional sets in the future.

Pretty awesome Fire Station set. Brio comes with other sets. This sets comes with two firemen, chainsaw, two tool boxes with hoses, one fire jelly, and a fire station slide. It was pre assembled and easy to plug in the slide. Set includes one wood track that can be connected to connect to the other sets and roads. One fire engine and one ladder trailer are included as well. Fire engine makes cute low decibel siren for about 7 seconds and turns off. Uses two button batteries beneath the engine truck. Roof top has helipad which can be played with a set with helicopter that Brio makes. Brio tracks are compatible with other wooden train sets made by other companies. It works with IKEA model and their trains sets. Plastics are sturdy and has wood surface on one side with texture. One fireman can ride in the fire engine. Ladder trailer has hose that is rolled on with string that can imitate rolling and unrolling. It will bring several years of imaginative plays for children. I enjoyed putting together. Can't wait to merge everything to existing train sets to table top city of imagination for my son who is 4.5 years old.

This BRIO Central Fire Station is a great addition to our numerous wooden track sets from generic to Chuggington to Thomas the Train. I love that it is compatible with all of the aforementioned sets, and that there’s a wooden track piece to attach to the firehouse so my boys (ages 4 and 7) can attach it to their other train track sets and make huge, fun tracks twisting all over the living room, and then the trains and fire trucks can pull right up to the fire station on the track.

This set is bright and colorful and made out of heavy duty, durable plastic with a bit of wooden trim on the front of the fire station. The details and the moveable arms on the two included firefighter figures far surpass the basic wooden people we’ve gotten with our more generic wooden train sets. This toy encourages lots of imaginative play, and it, along with our other train sets, really keeps my boys engaged and playing for quite a long length of time. This set is definitely a win in our house!

"BRIO Central Fire Station" is a fun, quality toy set; it's charmingly designed, with some fun features. However, this toy is simply too overpriced for what you get. This is at best a $40 item.

B01EARLQJ2.text: The Darth Vader TIE Fighter isn't exactly an aerodynamic shape, but Air Hogs managed to stay true to its form while making it reasonably flyable.  Compared to the underpowered RC X-Wing, this one has plenty of thrust provided by two tandem counter-rotating motors within the centerline duct.  You can maintain altitude with about 60% thrust.  After a few familiarization flights (and crashes), I was up to 100 feet flying wide circles searching for Rebel ships.  Level flight will requires a rather significant angle-of-attack, and with that pitch up attitude makes it look like it's being pulled along by an invisible string.  The compromise made in this design is a lot of wobble left and right (roll).  The thin rudder is just sufficient to provide controllable flight, though at times it looks more like a bat than a TIE fighter with the wobble  The trim knob does let you adjust the rudder's center position, but the right stick is not proportional, it's 3-position full left rudder, center rudder, and right rudder.  But all-in-all, this is true-to-form TIE Fighter that is flyable and fun out of the box.

B01J8X8K1K.text: These are a great learning too in teaching children  or anyone about time and how it works.  The pieces are durable and go together well.  The colors are great. I recommend these time rods.

This is a very inventive and colorful way to learn about time.  It also teaches a bit about fractions.  One hour is one long red rod.  Four shorter yellow 15-min rods also equal an hour, and when put together, they are the same length as the 1-hour rod.  This is especially helpful for kids who are more visually inspired.  It includes a teaching guide and six “workmats”.  Having a large “play clock” will come in handy as well (sold separately). Made in China.

These are a versatile and creative way to get young learners to conceptualize time.  You can use the activities in the guide or make up your own.  They are useful for those just learning time but are also handy to refresh and revitalize time and math activities for those that have moved on to more difficult levels.  We devised a few games and played in timed intervals. The kids were immediately touch and feel time segments” as if they were coins in a banking exercise. A great helper for impaired learners through advanced.  Recommended for home or class.

Pages are bound tight in the center via plastic as opposed to the d-ring style, which makes it easier to turn the pages and preventing cards from getting stuck and bent as they tend to do on d-ring pages. B01MZ21N0D.text: I love Wheel of Fortune and Bingo, but the Wheel of Fortune Bingo game is really not Wheel of Fortune or Bingo. You spin the wheel to determine what letter to cover with a cube. This is a Wheel of Fortune-inspired bingo.  It's okay. It's a simple concept so anyone who knows his/her letters can play. However, the cards with the Wheel of Fortune phrases are quite small and the tiny cubes that you use to place on top of letters (like bingo, but after spinning the wheel and landing on a series of letters) on the phrases are also really small. A bump sends the cubes off the card with no way of knowing which letters they were on, thus, making this game not quite ideal for younger ones who are fidgety or likely to bump their card.  This can potentially be addressed preventatively if you closely supervise little ones and ensure their card is somewhere that it won't get moved or accidentally bumped. Some of the phrases are long, so one round can take much longer than a round of bingo which can also be challenging for younger ones and a bit boring for older folks.

The actual game is garbage but my autistic son wanted it solely for the puzzles and he uses them in another version of the game.  The problem is that first off, the puzzles don't line up well inside the windows.  And then, it is cheaply constructed.  In our case the purchase suit our needs but I can't recommend this game to most folks.

This is an interesting spin on bingo. There are a large number of double-sided cards that have phrases on them. Like with blackout bingo, you have to cover all the letters of the card in order to win that round. The winner is the player with the most points after 3 rounds have been played. Each card has a set number of points it is worth if you win that round, and points can also be gained during each round by landing on the Jackpot space. Each space on the wheel is either a Jackpot, Bankrupt, Free Play or has 4 letters on it. If a player lands on a letter space, all players get to choose one letter to cover on their card. Each player can choose a different letter. If a player lands on a Free Play space, that player chooses any letter to cover on his/her card. The other players can also cover that letter on their cards if they have 2 or more of that letter. The Bankrupt spot requires the spinner to clear all the letters from the row with the most letters covered. There is a second side to the wheel which gives a variation to the game.

The game suggests it is for players 7+, but any child that recognizes letters and can follow directions can easily play this game. It does take a bit of time to play an entire game, though, and my 6 yr old grandson got bored rather quickly and decided not to play after the 1st round. Interestingly, he had done so well in the first round that he ended up wining the entire game!

The cards store neatly under the wheel, and the bags of cubes fit under there as well. The bags are not resealable and so I put the opened bags inside a ziploc sandwich bag. The wheel will only stay secure if the plastic cover is put on it and the game slid back into the box, so be sure and take care of the box.

There is enough variety to this game that it will remain a fun game for some time to come.

Large toys are always impressive but frankly this little doll is infinitely more practical. At 8.5 inches she is the perfect size for little kids. Additionally she is easy to take along on an outing. Had it been just slightly larger, it would have been easier to cuddle, there would be more movement of the limbs, more to hold on to and hug.

The body is fabric with a firm fill. The hands, feet, and face are vinyl and are firmly attached. The clothing is cotton and removes for washing (it has Velcro closures). Actually, the entire doll can be machine washed. Care has been taken that it has no small pieces. For example, the buttons are embroidered on, not actual buttons.

The face on the baby is very well drawn and attractive with a happy/alert expression, big blue eyes, and cute pouty lips. But two or three extra inches would have increased the possible range of movement, might have made the doll less stiff and cuddlier.

B01N5O9NRY.text: I use this in my ESL classes with various proficiency levels; this is a great warm-up / cool-down activity to get students brainstorming / using target vocabulary. You can adapt the cards / rules for various purposes; I use it to review thematic lessons or have students brainstorm as many words as possible on a given theme with a certain letter.

I have two teenagers who spend a lot of time in their rooms. We have the occasional game night once or twice a month for some quality family time. This game has become my 16 year old daughter's absolute favorite game. She has even started having her friends over for game night. You roll the dice and whatever letter comes up is the letter that each word that you write has to start with for that round. You are given a card that tells you what to write. For example, the card may say "a color" for number 1. The die was rolled and it landed on the letter G for that round. So you have to write down a color that starts with G on your list. Now if you and anyone else write the same G word, neither of you get a point. You are trying to come up with the most original and creative word that fits the letter and the subject. It's usually hard to come up with all twelve words in a round when the timer is set! We all enjoy this game!

I played this when I was a kid and it's still a great game if you only have 30 minutes to spare. In 30 minutes you can easily get in 3-4 rounds of brain busting fun. This game is really about trying to mentally out maneuver your friends by coming up with words starting with whatever letter the die at the beginning of the round gave you that are unique enough to answer the prompt that no one else has thought of it. If no one else thought of your answer you get a point and so on down the prompt card each round. If your answer is the same as someone else's you both cross it out and lose that potential point.

What I love about this game is the creativity in answers and how far you can bend the rules. We always play that the group votes on whether your answer is valid or allowable since it always gets a little fuzzy as the game goes on and our competitive nature picks up. It's a mental gymnastic type of game that is face paced and frustrating but over all lots of fun and laughs with a good group. A real classic that has great replayability.

Scattergories was one of my favorite games to play when I was younger, it made me feel like the adults when we played. Now that I am grown and older I find that I get just as excited to play as I did back then.

The concept of the game is super easy and you don't have to do a ton of explaining to teach someone who is new to it. I find that a lot of games out there today are super complicated, full of detailed instructions. Scattergories is simple, but engaging enough to still make it relevant today. This is a great team game but also good to play with individuals, both are equally exciting. Everyone is given a board with blank spaces to fill in along with a list of questions. The die is rolled and a letter is generated, from there you fill in the answers to the questions based on the letter that came up. Scoring is simple, with 2 points awarded to each unrepeated answer that starts with the letter that is rolled, 1 point for any unrepeated not starting with that letter, and a bonus point for answers that are two words starting with the rolled letter.

As I mentioned, this is a great party game and also family friendly. The questions, as far as I can remember are updated from editions in the past. This is sure to offer everyone a good time!

This set is a great toy for aspiring bakers, or sculptors. The molds, cut outs, and other tools are made with thick plastic for durability. The dough is organic and comes in three colors: yellow, red, and brown. The set has a cake stand and even forks and plates for serving creations! This is great for learning and imaginative play.

I think this is a really great set. It is so durable and is such a quality product. I love play-doh, but this set feels like it’s a better made product. It does cost more too, though. This is specialty green toy using recycled plastic and organic dough, so if you need those things in your toys this is great find.

The one drawback is to get more colors there is only a 4 pack, which is not cheap (red, blue, green, and yellow). To get additional colors beyond the 4 pack, like brown or pink, you would need additional sets. If all you want are more colors this isn’t the best deal. Hopefully the line will expand and there will be more options for consumers.

I like this product and am excited to see what else they introduce.

As with most Green Toys brand merchandise, I was quite impressed with the quality of materials on offer. Each mold and utensil was extremely sturdy and thick. Compared to the Play-Doh brand, the quality is much greater here for a comparable price. The dough itself is quite a bit softer than the Play-Doh brand - but not so soft that it would not retain a shape. It was a pleasure to work with. The dough has a lightly sweet scene, which is kind of concerning to me actually - I can imagine kids being interested in trying a bite here or there.

I do think there could have been some instructions put in the box, with some project ideas. When you open it up, it's kind of difficult to imagine where to begin.

Overall, for the price, this is a great buy that beats the quality of most Play-Doh brand products.

What a fun product! This soft colorful dough is so much fun to play with. It's wheat dough, so it smells different than other brands of dough on the market. All the plastic elements are made with recycled material, "100% post-consumer recycled plastic milk jugs (HDPE #2 plastic) that save energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions". Besides this, they make the dough using natural ingredients in a safe environment in the USA. Along with the 4 piece dough set, we picked up the Cake set. The cake set has molds to help you create your own culinary masterpieces out of the colorful clay. The only thing that I wish the molds had was some sort of indentation in them, to help you in taking the dough out without ruining your design. But overall, Green Toys makes great products and comes highly recommended!

I have bought many toys over the years for my six children.  Whenever I see a toy by Green Toys, I know that it is going to be quality!  I love that these toys are food safe, so when a pretend tea party or kitchen creation ends up using real food (like they often will) I can feel confident in the quality and safety of the materials.  These toys last much longer than others on the market, and they have gone through many children over the years.  Happy to add this to our collection.

This is a cute set. Price is a bit steep, but I am glad to have safer/healthier toys for my child. I do wish that there was another dough toy instead of the cutlery and plate, though. I felt that those were unneeded filler. The brown dough doesn't get utilized very much because it is a bit tough and crumbly. Other than those points I really like this set, and my child likes it, too.

My son loves this way more than the playdoh kitchen set he got for his birthday — it’s all the little details that make it. The molds make little tarts and pies that have great details on them, there’s a cake stand to put the “treats” on, etc. There’s also enough tools that 2-3 kids can play and everyone can have enough things to use, which is awesome.

The only downsides for me were that:

1) it doesn’t come with a rolling pin, and who makes playdoh pie without a rolling pin?

2) the little injector tool to squeeze out Star shapes is both a little too hard to use for small hands (not because of the force needed but because of the size), yet makes stars so tiny that they are barely recognizable as stars once you cut them off. So we mostly use it to make pointy snakes.

3) it includes “chocolate” colored play dough that truly looks like poop. Maybe there’s no way around this if you want “chocolate”, but we’ve stuck so far to using the playdoh we already had open in the house, and will keep these containers of dough on hand to use later.
really cute! the kids love it, makes a nice variety of stuff.  As sturdy as the playdoh equivalents.

B0725C6B4X.text: My family is into all kinds of video games, so I thought this might be fun to play with. My husband still has his original Atari 2600 console, but this is definitely easier to set up. There are only ten games on this emulator. Centipede was the closest to the actual game play in my husband's opinion. Some of the other games were more difficult to play because the joy stick doesn't have the track ball which the original Atari had and many of those games utilize that function. My husband thought the Asteroid game was neat because it was in color where it was originally in black and white. I let my 6 year old nephew play it and he did pretty well with it. I think it helped that he had never played the original and didn't know that the track ball even existed.

This works for the most part though Missile Command the screen keeps jumping around. There are only 10 games on this (and no way to add more) and not necessarily the best ones out there. Asteroids, Adventure, Missile Command, and Centipede are pretty well known and Canyon Bomber I remember came with the Atari 2600 my dad bought us back in the early 80s though I think Combat is better remembered. I don't really remember Crystal Castles or Warlords. It's kind of funny that Millipede actually looks worse than Centipede though I thought it was supposed to be the sequel.

My biggest problem is how stiff the control stick is. Even the original Atari 2600 I don't think was this stiff or surely my 7-year-old muscles could not have moved it around. And it's not very precise, which is important in games like Asteroids, Missile Command, and Breakout more so than Adventure. There are many of these products around or you can buy CD-ROMs or downloads of the old Atari games. I think Atari itself is even coming out with its own miniature system like the NES one that was so hot last year. That would probably be far better because it'll have more games and I think it's upgradeable to add more.

This would have been okay except for the fact that the stick control is so darn difficult to use. My teen daughter has a wrist injury and can't just it even with her brace on. It even made my hand/wrist tired and the neighbor's 5 year old also couldn't use it.

The games are much as remembered and this would be a fun half-gag gift for adults... with muscles. Now that Nintendo has opened it's arcade selection to it's Switch, we play there.

It's expensive. As of writing you need to pay as much for a single game as you would for a fancy coffee, and these are games you can download and play for free on any computer. A hundred times as many games could be included on modern memory for just a few cents. For this price you could buy a Raspberry Pi Zero computer board and a retro controller, and download thousands of games to play for free. Plus the Raspberry Pi setup would output in HDMI instead of RCA jacks.

It's got low-quality components. The joystick is stiff and unresponsive. It's like trying to stir dough with a wooden spoon. The real joystick is easier to move and more clicky, giving you some actual tactile response. I don't know how long this will last.

The connectors are bargain-basement. There are only 2 RCA jacks for video and audio, when any modern TV (if it even HAS jacks!) could make use of a third RCA jack for stereo sound. Even if they just sent the same audio out of two jacks you'd still get sound out of both sides of your speakers instead of one.

The game selection is okay, but some common games included in most packages aren't here. Yar's Revenge comes to mind. But it does have a lot of "top ten" classics, so there's no real stinker in the game selection.

When LEGO first started releasing sets for girls, the company got a lot of criticism for making things "too girly" -- more pink, shopping, and pets when LEGO used to be about building blocks for any gender. It's clear that LEGO has heard that criticism and is attempting to correct it with Olivia's Deluxe Bedroom. My seven-year-old daughter definitely approves.

Olivia is apparently some of a sci-fi geek, because she has a rocket-shaped bed, a huge gaming rig, a table, and a robot named Lobito. She also likes coffee -- a lot, because she has her own coffee table. I like to think it's also a robot named (the way the milk carton is positioned, it looks like it's meant to automatically pour into the cup), and I figure Olivia would probably program every single thing she could.

The game on Olivia's screen looks a little bit like Pac-Man as a heart, but the speakers next to the monitor speak volumes about how serious Olivia is about gaming. She has a super cute poster of a bunny on her wall, and above her is a place where Lobito hangs out. This is another hint as to Lobito's function, because one panel displays the temperature of coffee -- I'm pretty sure Lobito's job is to serve coffee for as long as Olivia stays up gaming.

My daughter put this entire set together herself without any help from me -- she slipped away into her room and came back out with the completed set one day. She then busted out her other LEGO sets and changed around some clothing (she wanted Olivia to wear a skirt) as well as some visitors to share coffee with. When I asked her to rate this set, she gave it five stars -- and that's high praise from someone who doesn't play that often with LEGO. Highly recommended for the awesome set and geek-girl-positive message!

My nephew is a Nerf connoisseur, with an arsenal that is the envy of most of the neighborhood kids, so I asked him to help me evaluate this new Nerf gun. He says that at the time he got it, it was new on the market, and he was excited to try it out. He found that it requires four D-batteries, which are not included, but fortunately his parents had some on hand. The gun was pretty big, but not unwieldy. The setup, he says, was pretty easy. After inserting the batteries, you simply insert the clip into the slot. Then insert your darts, and you are ready to fire. To fire, you pull the rev trigger, and then the trigger itself.

Compared to other blasters, my nephew found that despite its size, it is very customizable. It fires very fast and the loading feature is a big plus; it is unique to this particular blaster.

Holiday gift for my 6 year old -- and a waste of money. He got around 30 minutes of joy, because when it works it's kinda-sorta cool. But it takes too long to start firing, especially in the heat of battle, and it lacks enough power to send the darts very far.

The big problem is that this thing constantly jams, especially if the batteries start getting low. And this thing chews through batteries like few toys I've seen before. The jams are super frustrating, often tricky to resolve without doing any damage the gun or ruining the dart.

I've figured out through trial and error that this gun is very sensitive to dart width. I discovered quite by accident that some Nerf darts, even with the same color tips, have slightly different widths than some others. There are letter codes on the side of the dart that seem to correspond to which ones work better. The "J" ones we have seem to be okay, the "A" ones not so much. The difference is subtle, but you can tell when loading some of the manual guns, as some darts will offer more resistance. The tolerance is not an issue with those guns, but it's a huge problem with this one, as the wider darts consistently jam. Of course we don't have all of our darts sorted by 1mm width differences or tiny letters printed on the side of the tips, so every time my child wants to play with this gun we have to go through and check each dart one at a time to increase the odds that we'll have a good experience. That's ridiculous.

Nerf Elite Infinus review

My ProChrono Digital chronograph measured the speed of the darts fired (at peak rev) by this stock Elite Infinus blaster at an average of 72 feet per second (FPS) using Nerf Elite darts (it is capable of shooting any standard Nerf Elite darts; blue, green, white, orange, purple/grey, Starwars themed, Accustrike, and decorated Rebelle darts). The standard average velocity of a Nerf Elite blaster is 70 FPS, so it is on par with the rest of the Nerf Elite line. The bar set by this technological marvel that the Nerf engineers managed to create is something other toy manufacturers are going to have a hard time duplicating. This is because the Infinus allows the user to electronically feed darts from the top rear, traveling through the blaster, and directly into the drum (or whatever magazine is inserted at the time). This is pretty cool. There is an LED light above the dart feed port that shines solid yellow when it senses that your mag or drum is empty, solid green when it senses that a dart is ready to be fired, solid red when the jam access door is open, and blinks yellow when it senses that the magazine is at maximum capacity (and is unable to cram any more darts into it). I have to be honest, I doubted that this was possible to run smoothly because of the jams that happen so frequently in the Nerf Universe. But I have to say that I rushed the feeding mechanism, I used old battered and squashed darts, I overloaded it multiple times, and I even fed darts in backwards... and... no jams. None. It simply shot out whatever was in it, even the backwards darts (of course the darts inserted backwards did not fly well). I must say that I was very pleased at the smoothness of the Infinus’ operation. That said, I will now move on in my review of the rest of the blaster. This design screams heavy class, and it is on the heavy side. There are four 1.5v D alkaline batteries (not included) located in the rear shoulder-stock area of the blaster. This location helps to balance out the weight, evening the distribution from the handle so that it is not front-heavy due to the 30-dart drum. Because of the similar art design cues (tiger stripe camouflage embossed on the shell, blue, orange, black, grey plastic shell, etc.), I expected a repeat of the predecessor blaster, the Nerf Elite Hyperfire, but apparently the internals are closer in relation to the Nerf Elite Rapidstrike in that it has a dart-pusher feeding mechanism after it’s conveyor belt relays the dart from your fingertips and to a chamber above the magazine, which then activates another mechanism that pushes the dart down into to the magazine chamber. From there the blaster operates like the full-auto Rapidstrike. So it has the best of both worlds. The Hyperfire, with it’s high darts per second (DPS) ability, actually suffered from dart jams (including the shredding of darts) and it’s conveyor belt type dart feeding mechanism did not take well to modifications. I have not found any issues with the Infinus in regard to shredding or jams, and that is a good thing because opening the jam-access door reveals mostly an internal black plastic panel and an even smaller window which allows you to see about half the size of a dart. It would probably be very difficult to fish a dart out of such a small window. Anyway, moving on, the ergonomics are actually not that bad. The oversized angled fore-grip that is incorporated into the shell design is a comfortable way to hold the blaster while operating. It just gives a feeling of hollow plastic (there is a lot of dead space, so it actually is hollow plastic) when squeezed. The main pistol grip looks small in comparison to the bulk of the blaster’s body, but it is a decent size. The rev trigger is in close proximity to the mag/drum release button, but there is little chance of an accidental ejection because you need to give a little tug on the drum or magazine in order to remove it. I mean, you have to really shake it hard while holding the button down in order to drop the 30-dart drum without physically pulling it out, so no problems there. The main trigger operates as expected. The front barrel has a Nerf attachment point that allows you to add some barrel [drag] if you want. There are 2 Nerf tactical rails on the top of the blaster: one front and one in back; down the sight lines. There are 3 sling-mount attachment points: 1 under the barrel, the 2nd on the top of the shoulder-stock area, and the 3rd underneath it. For the aspiring young modders out there, I am fairly certain that the sensitive circuitry of this blaster will not be able to handle voltage modifications (Hasbro/Nerf frowns upon modifications to their products) without the proper checks and balances and electrical knowledge, expertise, or know-how to safeguard the circuitry from utter annihilation. The Nerf Elite Regulator’s circuit board was prone to frying, rendering it’s select-fire function useless, and it is highly likely that the Infinus’ dart loading function will also be controlled by a sensitive circuit board that is unprotected (that is, once you remove the thermistor). In conclusion, this is a fairly reasonably priced “flagship” blaster in the Nerf Elite line. If it is a one-trick pony, it is a terrific one-trick pony. I am thoroughly impressed at the flawlessness of the design, so my hat is off to you Nerf engineers. Thinking objectively, only real con in a sea of pros that the Infinus has is it’s sheer size and the heaviness that comes with it. Once past that, perhaps this is going to be the preferred blaster on the field of battle.

B0785HGLS6.text: My nieces and nephew (ages 4, 7, & 9) are obsessed with poop and poop toys. I thought they would have fun with this. I was right, they did. However, it was kind of a let down regarding the launcher. It didn't really launch the poop as expected. That didn't stop my nieces and nephew from lots of giggling. This is currently listed at $12.97 which I think is way over priced. This is something I would expect to see at a discount store at a discounted price.

I'm only giving it two stars because it gives me the giggles making up scatological puns and toilet humor when I look at it or show it to friends otherwise It'd be a solid one (see!) trending down (I can't stop!). I don't know what the final price will be, I've seen it insanely high and just ridiculously high. To be honest, if I saw the in the Dollar Store FOR a dollar and no more I'd buy a dozen and send them to my sillier friends. Beyond a great joke gift this is junk. I doubt it would hold a child's attention for more than a couple minutes tops. It's fairly cheap, thin plastic that topples easily. The seat won't stay up (just like a real toilet). The spring that's supposed to shoot your. . . scat in the air fires the moment you let go of it. There's no way you can press it down, drop in one of the two turds it comes with (see image), close the lid and 'watch it fly' as per the instructions. I've managed the task twice out of dozens of attempts. It's very easy to clog the toilet (see image) and even if you get it right it doesn't fly, it plops (I can't help myself) an inch or two away. The toilet lacks a handle, a small detail but one that would add realism. The figures they come with are sloppily painted. At anything more than a buck it's overpriced and suitable only as a joke gift. Be kind, don't give this to your kids.

Edit 01-22-18: Being serious for a moment here. I wanted to comment on the 'Squishy' description in the product's title. While this company may produce similar toys that are soft and pliable the ones that came with this toilet launcher are NOT. They are hard plastic and a potential choking hazard. The arms on the 'log' are especially fragile and could easily be broken off. I feel the four (4) year old age limitation set by the manufacturer is much too young. Please, use caution when giving this product to younger children. Thank you.

Who ever thought poop could be cute? It is! That little emoji that was a chocolate ice cream swirl that everyone decided was poop has got so many fans, that everyone wants some of the stuff. This set has two characters and a toilet. Put one of your characters in the toilet, flush and it goes flying out. You can flush any of the characters, but they won't go down the toilet, they pop out.

For whatever (odd) reason, the poo emoji has become ever-so-poopular over the last couple of years. I even received a putter (golf club) shaped like the emoji. Now everyone else is trying to grab onto the poop-train, such as this company.

Some will find these very funny and cute . . . . Others will not. Some kids think this sort of thing is simply hilarious, and they will love these. Just be forewarned that this item really doesn’t work as described. They don’t “fly out of the toilet”. . . .At best, they simply pop-out a little bit, and that’s if you leave the lid up.
It's silly--stupid even.  There's no shame in that, but it's poorly made and poorly executed.  Stuff flies everywhere, and nothing is worth picking up.  It's trash.

Let's pretend that it's a good idea to teach kids to play with poop and toilets.

Let's also pretend that this isn't made in the cheapest way possible, and pretend that when you fire the projectile in the air, it goes up, and comes straight down, back to where it started from.

Let's also pretend that the packaging is well printed and well constructed.

B079D7XHSZ.text: We played this recently with friends. There were six of us, 4 adults (2 couples) and two 17 year olds. The premise of the game was intriguing, but quickly lost our interest. We were not at home when we were playing, so that proved to be difficult. Many of the activity cards require you to go get something before you can begin the challenge. Items included a button down shirt, keys, a pen, and more. We had to keep skipping some of the challenges because we didn't have any access to the requested items. We did laugh a little and had fun, but when we were finished, we all just kind of agreed that it was just okay and none of us really had any interest in playing it again. The teens were amused by the tiny hands. I definitely think this game appeals more to teenagers and tweens than adults.

Well first, this game is absolutely ridiculous. Some of the challenges with the hands are near to impossible. But it did exactly what we hoping for at our last family reunion. It got several families blended into the fun and laughing hysterically, even those who had just driven 12 hours. The premise is easy, you have to do everything with Tiny or Tinier fake hands from catching a ball to acting out charades. The rules are simple although the rules of betting and scoring were less than clear to us. To be honest, we pretty much abandoned the betting and scoring of each round and just played the cards and the spinner. In the end we just declared the kids the winners.

Some things we learned.
- Put the score card well out of harms way. Ours was trod upon and score pieces were constantly tossed around.
- You cannot hold onto a pen with the hands like a baseball bat and swing it without impaling someone with the pen
- Give yourself lots of room
- The Charades part went over best.

Not sure how often this will come out, but it is a great leveler of ages and abilities and plays well in groups as long as kids are eight and up. It is kinetic, laugh producing and fun.

Games- Tiny Hands Challenge Children's Toy has all the things that make for a great game- it’s challenging, fun, moves fast and has plenty of hilarious laughter. The game comes with: 2 tiny hands, 2 tinier hands, 3 sets of activity cards (151 total), 20 scoring tokens, 1 spinner, 1 string (shoe lace), 1 ball, 1 sand timer (time is one minute), 1 wager mat and instructions. You can play with 4-10 players and recommended age is 8 and up.

You begin by dividing into 2 teams- yellow and blue. You set up the wager mat and the 3 decks of cards. Then set out the hands, spinner, string, ball and sand timer. You play rock, paper, scissors to see who goes first. You spin the spinner to see which activity card you will do and which hands you will do it with- tiny or tinier. Some of the activities use pens, paper, cups and coins, so you will want to have these items available too.

Once you know what activity you must do with which hands, you make a wager. If you lose, your opponent gets the token points. Even if you win, your opponent can challenge you. The 3 sets of cards are: Solo, Pair and Charades. The timer being one minute long makes the challenges and charades almost impossible to finish in such a short time. Luckily, some of the challenges don’t use the timer and give you multiple tries. There is also a Face Off, where both teams do a challenge at the same time. Doing the challenges and charades in such a short time with these tiny hands is almost impossible and laughing so hard totally impossible. The first team to collect 31 token points wins. Great Fun, Challenges and Laughter. 5 STARS.

This is a fun playset that's relatively easy to put together though it isn't without it's quirks. Here are the pros and cons of this set as I see them.
Pros:
* Fun. This playset is actually quite a lot of fun. There are tons of ramps, an alternate ramp configuration, lights and sounds, and is compatible with all Hot Wheels-type cars and trucks.
* CB radio handset. Not only controls the lights and sounds but also acts like a microphone to act like you're actually on a CB radio. Very fun.
* Cars included. Ok, its a sort-of fire truck and a police helicopter.
* Stickers are easy to apply, look great and really make the set pop.
* Easy to assemble. Directions are clear and pieces are marked.

Cons:
* Cheap feeling. Matchbox has been the down market car brand ever since Mattel bought them so they could differentiate it from Hot Wheels. The cars and the whole set just has a low price feel to it and easily the biggest drawback of this set. This goes for the included cars as well.
* Narrow and a little tipsy. The set is very narrow and kept upright by the ramps that while connect together easily enough, with rough play the connections aren't strong enough to keep it upright.
* Designed come out the box easily though I think they need to keep working on that though it isn't the biggest issue.

Summary.
This really is a fun set despite is very budget feel. It's easy to put together, the ramps are fun and it does pop visually. Just be aware of the cheap feel and keep expectations in check.

If you don't use highlighters basically constantly, then these might last longer and be in nicer shape for you! If you use them as much as you use other pens, then save yourself the heartache of seeing a color you love fade into nothing within a week.

Green toys have long been a favorite in our family. The durable nature, use of recycled materials, and Made in the USA are selling points, but it is the fact that our sons universally love them that really make them winners. With spring finally coming out, this set seemed like it would be fun, and it certainly brought out the interest in our burgeoning gardeners. It even inspired my older son to ask me, "Do you remember when I loved Elmo," which is hilarious sinec he's never loved Elmo. The power of suggestion is an amazing thing.

This kit did a great job in variety. There are three mini flower pots, three earth beds (although I'd recommend augmenting with some potting soil, basil, carrot and sunflower seeds, seed markers so you remember what's in each pot, four sheets of stickers (because what small child doesn't love stickers) and a mini activity book. We also got the [[ASIN:B07BBBJXMR Green Toys Sesame Street Watering Can-Elmo Childrens Basic Skills Development Toys]], which nicely complimented this set and continued the Sesame Street theme.

There was a fair amount of overlap in this set's activity book and the other sets, but overall, this did a great job of inspiring interest in my 3 and 6 year old sons who are eagerly awaiting the sprouting of their plants!
Love this! My 4 year old thought this was so fun. All three plants grew, and we're now transferring the sunflowers to a bigger pot. These were fun, easy and the pots are durable plastic.

I am not an arts and crafts kind of mom. I am not a vegetable garden mom. With that out of the way we absolutely enjoyed every bit of this, especially my 3 1/2 year old son, who cannot follow directions or sit still to save his life. We had been reading a book about seeds and gardening so this seemed like an activity we should try since April was just around the corner.

The directions are very simple. The only thing I changed was the order in which the stickers went on the pot. I recommend making that the very first activity you do. That way you can talk about what you're going to do with the soil and seeds while having fun placing stickers all over the CLEAN EMPTY pots.

Then we added the soil pucks and water. My son loved watching it expand. You have to wait 20 minutes so we turned to the included coloring book and did activities in there while we waited for the soil to expand. It does not come with a trowel or rake. We tried using a rusty trowel we had lying around in the garage (like I said, not a gardener) which wasn't very ergonomic. Honestly a fork would do just as well to mix the soil and pat it down. Surprisingly, I did not have soil all over my kid and the kitchen so A+ for being a "clean" dirty craft.

Then you poke 5-6 one inch deep holes with your finger (fun!) and add seeds. The sunflower seeds were big enough for my son to handle. However, his fine motor skills were not advanced enough to handle the microscopically small basil and carrot seeds so I did those. Each packet comes with more seeds than you can plant at once so this is something you can do again once the first batch is grown out. We placed the pots on our windowsill and waited.

It worked! We got carrots, basil, and sunflowers. Every morning we'd take them down so he could look inside and see how much bigger they got. It was so nice to do something earthy and crafty since I don't love my children enough to do those things on a regular basis. Kidding. Anyway, it's worth noting that the materials including the packaging are made from recycled goods and a lot of this stuff can be recycled again.

Overall this was an easy, simple to follow activity that was educational, fun, and hands-on that can be done indoors or out. I think this would also make a great gift for a child 3-6 years old.

*If you found my review helpful please click 'yes' below. Thanks!*
Great! My daughter loved this set, started growing and poping up within days, and now a month later still growing strong in our garden!

This is a great activity for children. Young children who want to garden, or those who wish to teach young children about gardening or plants should get this set. It is almost completely self-contained (you need water and a trowel). It is so simple to use.

The kit comes with three pots and three soil discs. You can decorate the pots with provided stickers, then put the soil discs in the pots and add 1 cup of water. After 30 minutes, the soil will have expanded. Now you need to find a trowel and break up the soil. You make a whole and add 5 seeds for basil, carrots, or sunflowers. Then you cover and pat down the soil, add the marker so you remember what is growing, and water the seeds. Place the pot in the sun and continue to care for the plants with watering and sunlight. Then watch it grow!

It really is simple and can be done quickly and without a mess. The pots are thick and sturdy. The colors are cute and cheerful in pink, purple, and yellow. The stickers for decorating are Elmo, Abby, Bert, Ernie, Cookie Monster, Big Bird, Oscar the Grouch, Grover, and some insects and plants, too. The box it all comes in is very beautiful with full color pictures all over. There are plenty of seeds to plant in your own pots, or for next year. I just wish they gave you a trowel in the box! Recommended

B07C8T3PH9.text: My daughter received several unikitty lego sets for Christmas, and I have to say she just loves them. Unikitty being her favorite, it's great that lego expanded these sets with several new characters. Definitely an 8 year olds imagination going wild!

This LEGO UNIKITTY CLOUD CAR BUILDING KIT (126 Piece) is a small kit that an adult can assemble in half an hour; the building techniques are simple and straightforward, so that small children shouldn’t find it difficult.

There are two elements that I particularly like, both on Unikitty’s cloud car--a propeller that spins with a flick of the finger, and a pair of spring-loaded “sparkle matter” guns that fire dots when you press the catch on the special LEGO gun element. I also like the use of a blue crystal element that becomes a fountain in a tiny park.

The figures have their faces printed on special bricks (no stickers). Unikitty has a wide, open-mouthed grin; her head turns, and she fits in a space in the cloud car. Other figures are Square Bear and Feebee.

Princess Unikitty was introduced in “The LEGO Movie”. At first I thought that a hybrid unicorn/cat was creepy, but now I’m totally charmed by the “Unikitty” TV series that airs on the Cartoon Channel, and by the LEGO Unikitty sets. I only wish that the Unikitty minifigs with different versions of Unikitty (see [[ASIN:B07BMF3K48 Unikitty Add-On Item]] were marketed as a straightforward collection, instead of as expensive grab-bag “mystery figures”.
Tiny pieces!

I find the build itself a little disposeable although he really loved building it.  I would expect the pieces to be quickly incorporated into his own creations, but for now they have a place of honor on the display shelves.  All in all a small but nice set.
